info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.3: LLM-Assisted Transcription: Hallucination, Bias, and the Specialization Gap.

name.text: 01 Question: Today's Question

questiontext.text: What is today's comparison actually asking about the three transcriptions?

generalfeedback.text: The question is not which system is best but what kind of error each makes — the kinds differ more than the rates.

answer.text: What each system does when it goes wrong, and what that reveals about the kind of system it is.

feedback.text: Correct. A program producing letter-strings that are not words and one producing smooth invented Greek have failed very differently.

answer.text: Which of the three produced the lowest error rate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rate is part of it, but the kinds of failure matter more to an editor than the totals.

answer.text: Whether the AI model can replace the manual step entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual step is needed as a reference regardless — that was Tuesday's argument.

answer.text: Which system is fastest to set up and run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cost is recorded and does matter, but it is not what the comparison is *for*.

name.text: 02 Question: What These Models Are

questiontext.text: Why is a general AI model's deep knowledge of language a liability when transcribing a manuscript?

generalfeedback.text: A VLM's linguistic knowledge is its strength on modern text and its liability on manuscripts, because it resolves ambiguous ink by expectation.

answer.text: It brings that knowledge to bear on unclear ink, and settling unclear evidence by expectation is exactly what a diplomatic transcription must not do.

feedback.text: Correct. Its greatest strength on modern text is its worst liability on your page.

answer.text: It makes the model slower, because it checks every reading against its vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is one of its advantages, not a cost.

answer.text: It causes the model to refuse readings it considers ungrammatical.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not refuse — it supplies something plausible instead, which is worse.

answer.text: It restricts the model to languages well represented in modern writing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will attempt any language. The problem is what it produces when the ink is unclear.

name.text: 03 Question: The Specialization Gap, in Numbers

questiontext.text: What is the most striking thing about GPT-4o's 1.39% on modern English and 52.23% on historical English?

generalfeedback.text: The same model achieves 1.39% CER on modern handwriting and 52.23% on historical — the gap is period, not language.

answer.text: It is the same model on the same language — only the century differs.

feedback.text: Correct. That isolates the cause: the training material contains a great deal of modern handwriting and very little old handwriting.

answer.text: It shows historical English is harder to read than modern English for anyone, human or machine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Palaeographers read it well. The gap is about what the model was exposed to.

answer.text: It shows the historical sample was photographed at a lower resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing indicates that, and the pattern holds across several datasets.

answer.text: It shows the model performs better when given more context to work with.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It had a full page in both cases.

name.text: 04 Question: Making Things Look Older Than They Are

questiontext.text: What is over-historicization, and why is it not a simple misreading?

generalfeedback.text: GPT-4o beat a generic HTR baseline on CER while inventing anachronistic characters in 59% of files — the metric and the fidelity diverge.

answer.text: The model inserts characters from an *earlier* period than the document, because it has learned that old documents go with old spelling.

feedback.text: Correct. It is not misreading the ink; it is reading its own expectation of the period.

answer.text: The model refuses to modernize spelling even when asked to, producing archaic output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would at least be faithful to the page. Here it invents forms that are on no page at all.

answer.text: The model dates the manuscript too early in any commentary it produces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem is in the transcription itself, not in dating.

answer.text: The model preserves archaic characters that a specialist model would drop.

feedback.text: Incorrect — it is the opposite. It adds characters that were never there.

name.text: 05 Question: Why One Score Is Not Enough

questiontext.text: Why is the usual character score inadequate for judging a historical transcription?

generalfeedback.text: A model can score well on CER while silently modernizing or hallucinating archaism — check preservation and insertion separately.

answer.text: It treats every difference as equal, so inventing a period spelling counts the same as any other substitution.

feedback.text: Correct. A model can score well while wrecking precisely the evidence the transcription exists to hold.

answer.text: It cannot be computed at all when line breaks have been lost.

feedback.text: Incorrect — that is a practical difficulty, and a real one, but not the argument here.

answer.text: It is calculated on words rather than characters, which hides letter-level errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is calculated on characters. The word-level figure is a separate measure.

answer.text: It only works when both texts are in the same language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a string comparison and is indifferent to language.

name.text: 06 Question: Mess, Chat, and Confident Gap-Filling

questiontext.text: Why is losing the line breaks a practical disaster and not just untidy?

generalfeedback.text: VLMs reflow lines, add commentary, and fill gaps confidently — none of which announces itself in the output.

answer.text: Without them you cannot match the output to your image boxes, cannot train on it, and cannot compare it line by line against your own version.

feedback.text: Correct. Wednesday's model produced line-by-line output because it worked on line strips; today's sees a whole page and hands back prose.

answer.text: Because TEI cannot encode a paragraph that has no line breaks in it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It encodes continuous prose perfectly well. The loss is in what you can do with it.

answer.text: Because the line breaks carry the accents, which are lost with them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accents are unaffected by reflowing.

answer.text: Because the word count changes when lines are run together.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The words are the same; only the arrangement changes.

name.text: 07 Question: Setting Up a Fair Test

questiontext.text: Why record the exact instruction and the model version, not just the result?

generalfeedback.text: Record the prompt verbatim, the model version, and the date — without them the result is not reproducible.

answer.text: A different wording or a quietly updated model gives a different number, so without them nobody — including you — can repeat the result.

feedback.text: Correct. These services change without announcing it, which is why the date matters too.

answer.text: Because the instruction must be submitted for approval before the assignment is marked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No approval step exists. The reason is reproducibility.

answer.text: Because the model will refuse to run twice with the same instruction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will run as often as you like.

answer.text: Because the version number determines which credits are charged.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No credits are involved on Friday, and that is part of the cost comparison.

name.text: 08 Question: Writing the Instruction

questiontext.text: Why does the recommended instruction spell out every constraint, rather than just asking for a transcription?

generalfeedback.text: Every constraint in the prompt addresses a documented failure mode, and a good prompt reduces those failures without eliminating them.

answer.text: Each line addresses a documented failure — chat, reflowed lines, spelled-out short forms, modernized spelling, confidently filled gaps.

feedback.text: Correct. And even so it only reduces those failures; you still check the output against every requirement.

answer.text: Because longer instructions always produce more accurate output from these models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not the virtue — targeting known failures is.

answer.text: Because the model will otherwise refuse to transcribe Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will attempt it readily. The problem is the form the attempt takes.

answer.text: Because the constraints are required for the output to validate as TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output is plain text; encoding it comes later.

name.text: 09 Question: Running It

questiontext.text: Why resist adjusting the wording until the output looks good?

generalfeedback.text: Commit the raw output before correcting or reformatting anything — that state is what Week 5 measures.

answer.text: You would end up with an instruction tuned to this one passage, which is not what you set out to measure.

feedback.text: Correct. Run the planned test, and note any extra attempts separately.

answer.text: Because each attempt consumes credits from the shared class allowance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Friday's tool needs no credits — that is part of why it looks cheap.

answer.text: Because the model performs worse each time it is asked the same thing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not degrade with repetition.

answer.text: Because only the first attempt may be committed to the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commit each separately, with its own labels.

name.text: 10 Question: Reading the Output Sceptically

questiontext.text: Why can the most serious errors not be found by reading the output carefully?

generalfeedback.text: Fluent output reads as correct, so check against the image — and look specifically at where you recorded damage.

answer.text: Smooth text reads as correct, and the mistakes that matter most are the ones that read perfectly — you have to compare against the picture.

feedback.text: Correct. Look especially at the damaged patch you identified in Lesson 3.2.

answer.text: Because the output is too long to read carefully in one session.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not the obstacle; plausibility is.

answer.text: Because the errors are concentrated in the accents, which are hard to see on screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accent loss is one problem among several, and it is visible once you look.

answer.text: Because the model marks its own errors, so reading is unnecessary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its self-marking is unreliable, as the next section shows.

name.text: 11 Question: It Does Not Know What It Does Not Know

questiontext.text: Suppose the model's uncertainty flags turn out to be unrelated to where it actually went wrong. What follows?

generalfeedback.text: If the model's uncertainty markers do not track its errors, you must check everything — and the tool saves no verification labour at all.

answer.text: You must check all of it, so the tool saves you no checking work at all — whatever it saves in typing.

feedback.text: Correct. That bears directly on whether the method is usable for your manuscript.

answer.text: You should re-run it with a stricter instruction about marking uncertainty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem is that these models judge their own confidence poorly, not that the instruction was too loose.

answer.text: The flags can be ignored and the confident readings trusted.

feedback.text: Incorrect — that is precisely backwards. Confident readings over damage are the most serious finding.

answer.text: It means the image resolution was too low for the model to judge.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Poor self-assessment is a property of these models, not of your images.

name.text: 12 Question: Is It Reading, or Reciting?

questiontext.text: How can you tell whether the model read your page or recited a printed edition from memory?

generalfeedback.text: Where your manuscript differs from the printed text, a model reciting from memory gives the printed reading — that is the test.

answer.text: Look at a place where your copy differs from the standard text — reading gives your copy's reading, reciting gives the printed one.

feedback.text: Correct. The damage test supports it: filling an illegible patch fluently *and correctly* is more damning than filling it wrongly.

answer.text: Ask the model whether it has seen the text before.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its self-report is unreliable, as section 11 established.

answer.text: Compare the output's length against your transcription's.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length tells you nothing about the source of the words.

answer.text: Check whether the output preserves the line breaks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That tests whether it followed instructions, not whether it read the ink.

name.text: 13 Question: A Rough Score

questiontext.text: Why normalize both texts before working out a score?

generalfeedback.text: Normalize both strings to NFC before computing CER, or you measure encoding difference rather than transcription difference.

answer.text: Accents can be stored in two different ways, and comparing one storage form against the other measures storage rather than transcription.

feedback.text: Correct. The inflation can be severe, and it has nothing to do with how well anything was read.

answer.text: Because the score requires both texts to be the same length.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It handles different lengths by design — that is what the edit count is for.

answer.text: Because Greek cannot be compared character by character without normalization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can; the risk is that identical-looking characters are stored differently.

answer.text: Because normalization removes the chat and preamble automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stripping the chat is a separate step you do yourself.

name.text: 14 Question: Where These Tools Genuinely Help

questiontext.text: What distinguishes the tasks these models are good at from the ones they are bad at?

generalfeedback.text: These tools help where linguistic knowledge is the point and harm where it contaminates evidence — transcription is the second kind.

answer.text: They help where knowing language is the point, and harm where knowing language contaminates the evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Transcription is the second kind — which is why translating a transcription you already have is a perfectly good use.

answer.text: They help with short tasks and struggle with long ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not the dividing line — a whole-page translation is fine.

answer.text: They help with modern material and struggle with anything written by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They do very well on modern handwriting. The difficulty is historical material.

answer.text: They help when given examples and struggle without them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem is structural, not a matter of how many examples are supplied.

name.text: 15 Question: Where That Leaves the Method

questiontext.text: If the general model scores above 15% and your trained model below it, what is the right conclusion?

generalfeedback.text: Automation saves labour only below the threshold where correction costs less than transcription — and you have now measured where your tools sit.

answer.text: That the specialized tool is the right one for this job — and you now have your own measurement to say so.

feedback.text: Correct. Not that AI is useless, but that this task, on this material, is better served by the specialist.

answer.text: That AI models are unsuitable for humanities research generally.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a sweeping claim your measurement does not support.

answer.text: That the general model needs a better instruction and should be re-run until it improves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuning until it looks good is the trap section 09 warned about.

answer.text: That your trained model is accurate enough to use without correction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Below 15% means correcting is worthwhile, not that correcting is unnecessary.

name.text: 16 Question: Recording AI Use in the Repository

questiontext.text: Why does the date you used the model matter as much as its version number?

generalfeedback.text: Record the model access date — a hosted model can change without notice, making the date the only record of what produced the output.

answer.text: These services run on somebody else's computers and can change overnight without the version number moving.

feedback.text: Correct. The date is often the only record of what actually produced your text.

answer.text: Because the assignment requires all work to be dated for marking purposes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is reproducibility, not administration.

answer.text: Because model output is only valid for a limited period after generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output does not expire. What changes is the system behind it.

answer.text: Because the date determines which version of TEI the output conforms to.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output is plain text and conforms to nothing until you encode it.

name.text: 17 Question: Putting the Three Side by Side

questiontext.text: Which lines should the three-way comparison concentrate on, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Compare on the lines where you recorded uncertainty — agreement on easy lines is uninformative, and divergence on hard lines is the finding.

answer.text: The lines where you recorded doubt or damage, because what each system does when the evidence runs out is the finding.

feedback.text: Correct. Agreement on easy lines tells you almost nothing.

answer.text: The first ten lines, so the sample is consistent across students.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A fixed position is arbitrary; the informative lines are the difficult ones.

answer.text: The lines where all three agree, since agreement confirms the reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Agreement on easy lines is exactly the uninformative case.

answer.text: The lines with the most abbreviations, since those dominate the score.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Worth including, but the criterion is where *you* recorded uncertainty.

name.text: 18 Question: Sorting the Mistakes

questiontext.text: Four kinds of failure belong almost entirely to the general AI. What do they have in common?

generalfeedback.text: The VLM's distinctive failures are not recognition errors but consequences of being a language model — and the HTR model cannot make your expectation-driven errors.

answer.text: None of them is a reading mistake — they follow from it being a language machine pointed at a reading job.

feedback.text: Correct. It reformats because it writes prose, chats because it converses, and invents because it completes.

answer.text: They all come from the image being supplied at too low a resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They occur at any resolution, because they arise from what the system is.

answer.text: They all appear only when the instruction was poorly written.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A good instruction reduces them; it does not remove them.

answer.text: They are all caused by the model having seen the printed text before.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reciting from memory is a separate failure, tested for separately.

name.text: 19 Question: Reporting a Result That Did Not Work

questiontext.text: Why is a documented failure a contribution rather than a failed assignment?

generalfeedback.text: A documented failure — this model, this prompt, this manuscript, this rate — is a contribution, and vague dismissal is not.

answer.text: This model, this instruction, this manuscript, this score — that record saves the next person from repeating the attempt.

feedback.text: Correct. Reporting only what worked is the opposite of what is wanted.

answer.text: Because negative results are marked more generously than positive ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The value is scholarly, not a marking concession.

answer.text: Because a failed attempt proves the tool should never be used for anything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The honest conclusion is narrow and specific, not a blanket judgement.

answer.text: Because the assignment only requires that something was attempted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It requires a specific, defensible conclusion about your own material.

name.text: 20 Question: Working Remotely Today

questiontext.text: Why might your accent-fixing hook not run today, even though it worked all week?

generalfeedback.text: Hooks are not cloned — install and test your NFC hook on this machine before committing anything today.

answer.text: Hooks live in `.git/hooks/`, which is not copied when you clone — so a fresh copy has none.

feedback.text: Correct. Install it from your tracked `tools/` folder and test it before committing anything.

answer.text: Hooks are disabled automatically when git runs outside the campus network.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git neither knows nor cares which network you are on.

answer.text: Hooks expire after a set number of commits and must be reinstalled.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They do not expire. They were simply never copied across.

answer.text: Hooks only run on files that have been pushed to the remote.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They run before a commit is recorded, locally.

name.text: 21 Question: What This Week Established

questiontext.text: What do all eight of the week's findings have in common?

generalfeedback.text: Every finding in the table is a measurement against a hand-produced ground truth — which is the week's thesis in operation.

answer.text: Every one is a measurement taken against a reference that somebody made by hand.

feedback.text: Correct. That is the week's thesis in operation — automation speeds the work and depends absolutely on the hand-made reference.

answer.text: Every one shows that specialized tools outperform general ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Several do, but others concern transfer learning, layout, and pipeline design.

answer.text: Every one was produced by this course rather than drawn from published work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are published findings, which you have now partly repeated yourself.

answer.text: Every one concerns Greek manuscripts specifically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They span Latin, English, German, and Russian material.

name.text: 22 Question: Checklist Before You Finish

questiontext.text: Which check on today's list would catch a failure that nothing else on it would?

generalfeedback.text: For a well-known text, the memorization test is the most important check available — nothing else detects a recited printed edition.

answer.text: The test for reciting — a model reproducing a printed edition from memory produces excellent-looking output that is worthless as a record of your copy.

feedback.text: Correct. It applies only to well-known texts, but where it applies nothing else detects it.

answer.text: The line count, since a mismatch invalidates every later comparison.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Serious, but it is conspicuous — you notice immediately.

answer.text: The score calculation, since an unnormalized comparison inflates the figure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Also serious, and also detectable by other means.

answer.text: The provenance labels, since unlabelled machine text cannot be identified later.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Important, but the audit commands would reveal a missing label.

name.text: 23 Question: Looking Ahead to Week 5

questiontext.text: Why does Week 5 lose nothing by having only two meetings?

generalfeedback.text: Week 5 double-keys the ground truth and then measures against it — and the Transcription Assignment on October 2 includes the reconciliation report.

answer.text: Reconciliation *is* the comparison, so the two meetings — typing it twice, then measuring — cover the week's work.

feedback.text: Correct. Wednesday 30 September is closed for Truth and Reconciliation.

answer.text: Because the measurement is done automatically and needs no meeting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Friday's meeting is the measurement, done properly and line by line.

answer.text: Because the Transcription Assignment is due before the missing meeting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is due Friday 2 October, at the end of that week.

answer.text: Because Week 5 repeats Week 4 and can be shortened safely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does new work: improving the reference, then measuring against it.

name.text: 24 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What separates a good conclusion from a poor one in today's report?

generalfeedback.text: A specific measured conclusion about *your* manuscript is the deliverable; a general claim about AI is a repetition of what you were told.

answer.text: Naming the actual script, resolution, model, and figures, rather than making a general claim about AI.

feedback.text: Correct. The general claim repeats what you were told; the specific one is something you established.

answer.text: Reaching a conclusion that agrees with the published benchmarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Agreement is not the standard — a result that contradicts them, properly measured, is more interesting.

answer.text: Recommending that the specialized tool be used for the rest of the term.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That may well follow, but the recommendation is not what makes the conclusion good.

answer.text: Keeping the conclusion short enough to fit the report's word limit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Specificity, not brevity, is what is being asked for.

name.text: 25 Question: Choosing Tools for the Rest of the Term

questiontext.text: What should you not do with your trained model's output from Week 6 onward?

generalfeedback.text: Let today's measurement set your tool choices for the term, and record the reasons at the time rather than reconstructing them later.

answer.text: Pass it through an AI to clean up, which is documented to make the result worse.

feedback.text: Correct. It cannot see the picture, so it corrects toward the ordinary — damaging precisely the unusual readings you are recording.

answer.text: Correct it by hand, since corrections introduce your own expectation errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Correcting by hand against the image is exactly the intended workflow.

answer.text: Commit it to the repository before it has been checked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is required — raw output must be committed unchecked so it can be scored.

answer.text: Use it to extend the transcription onto further leaves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the point of having trained it, provided it scores well enough.

name.text: 26 Question: The Bigger Point

questiontext.text: Why does the three-step cycle collapse if the manual step is done badly?

generalfeedback.text: The three-step cycle is a general method for evaluating tools against material, and it collapses if the manual reference is compromised.

answer.text: Every measurement is a distance from the reference, so a damaged reference damages everything computed from it.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why Tuesday is not a warm-up.

answer.text: Because the specialized tool cannot be trained without a perfect transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It trains on imperfect material readily — the problem is what the results then mean.

answer.text: Because the AI step is run first and depends on the manual output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The AI step is last, and needs no input from you but a picture.

answer.text: Because the comparison requires all three to have the same error rate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They will differ enormously, and that difference is the finding.

name.text: 27 Question: Counting the Cost Honestly

questiontext.text: Why might typing by hand beat the trained model for a passage of twenty to forty lines?

generalfeedback.text: For a short passage, HTR's setup cost may never amortize — say so if you find it, because the measurement is the point.

answer.text: The trained model costs a whole session to set up, and across so few leaves that setup never pays for itself.

feedback.text: Correct. Say so if you find it — the value is in having measured the trade-off on real material.

answer.text: Because the trained model is less accurate than a person on short passages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy does not depend on passage length. The argument is about setup cost.

answer.text: Because short passages cannot supply enough examples to train anything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One leaf is enough for a first model — the issue is whether the effort repays.

answer.text: Because the platform charges a minimum fee regardless of passage length.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The cost being counted is your time, not a fee.

name.text: 28 Question: Committing and Pushing

questiontext.text: What is easy to forget when pushing at the end of today, and why does it matter?

generalfeedback.text: Push tags explicitly — they are not pushed by default, and Week 5's measurement retrieves the tagged states.

answer.text: Tags are not pushed by default, and Week 5's measurement fetches the three tagged versions.

feedback.text: Correct. A tag that exists only on this laptop is one Week 5 cannot use from anywhere else.

answer.text: Commits are not pushed unless each is pushed individually.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A single push sends all commits on the branch.

answer.text: The provenance labels must be added again after pushing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are part of the commit message and travel with it.

answer.text: Raw output must be pushed to a separate branch from corrections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Separate commits, not separate branches.

name.text: 29 Question: Pulling the Week Together

questiontext.text: State the thesis that ties all three meetings of this week together.

generalfeedback.text: Three meetings, one thesis — automation accelerates transcription and depends absolutely on a hand-produced reference to be evaluated at all.

answer.text: Automation genuinely speeds the work and depends absolutely on a hand-made reference, because that is the only thing its errors can be measured against.

feedback.text: Correct. Tuesday built the reference, Wednesday measured a bounded tool against it, Friday an unbounded one.

answer.text: Automated transcription is not yet good enough for scholarly work and should be avoided.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The specialized model may do very well. The claim is about what makes evaluation possible.

answer.text: Specialized tools are always better than general ones for every task.

feedback.text: Incorrect. General models excel at several tasks, including translating an existing transcription.

answer.text: Manual transcription is the most accurate method available.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It contains errors too — which is why Week 5 types the page a second time.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Reading Well Is Not Reading Right

questiontext.text: Why are the specialized model's loud, obvious failures described as a virtue?

generalfeedback.text: Fluency and fidelity are independent, and the more plausible a tool's output, the less its plausibility tells you about its accuracy.

answer.text: Output that announces its own doubt by being obviously wrong is safer than output that hides its doubt by being smooth.

feedback.text: Correct. An impossible letter string tells you something true about the ink; a perfect word tells you about the model's expectations.

answer.text: Because obvious failures are easier for the platform to correct automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing corrects them automatically — they are easy for *you* to see.

answer.text: Because they occur less often than the general model's failures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They may occur more often. Conspicuousness, not frequency, is the virtue.

answer.text: Because they indicate the model is close to the right reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They indicate the ink was genuinely unclear, not that the answer is nearly right.
